When authors share their data and analysis code, the idea is that anyone should be able to run that code on that data and get the results reported in the paper. But sharing data and code in a way that results are reproducible is difficult, and researchers have often not received training in how to share data and code. As a consequence, there are often basic mistakes in public repositories that stand in the way of computationally reproducible results. Automated checks can help researchers identify and fix these mistakes, such as not sharing all files that are loaded in code, using absolute instead of relative filepaths, using values that are not computed in the code that is shared, changing file names so they no longer match the code, or not loading all libraries. 

Checking whether data and code is reproducible is tedious. It also often requires repeated back and forths between the person performing the checks, and the researchers sharing data and code. Ideally, checks do not just focus on whether code runs, but also whether all results in a manuscript are reproduced by the code, but this takes a lot of time. 

Metacheck's `reproducibility_check` module attempts to perform all these checks automatically. When it succeeds, researchers and/or reviewers, data managers, or editors know that data and code is shared in a reproducible manner, and they do not need to perform manual checks. This saves everyone time, and leads to data and code repositories that are more useful for science. Our reproducibility check module is completely code-based. It uses no AI: when it runs the modules it builds on, such as `data_check`, it turns the use of a large language model off for them, also when you have set `llm_use(TRUE)`. It can run locally on your computer without sending information to an external server.

This chapter starts with the module at work on two versions of the same small study: one where every reported result can be reproduced, and one where several cannot. The sections after the example describe each step of the check in detail.

## Computationally reproducing a simple Stroop experiment

Both papers analyse the same classroom data from Daniël Lakens's introduction to psychology and technology course. Students named the ink color of words that matched the color (the word "red" printed in red) and of words that did not (the word "red" printed in green), and reported the time they needed in seconds. Both papers report four results: the mean and standard deviation of the reaction times in each condition, the correlation between the reaction times in the two conditions, a paired *t*-test for the Stroop effect, and a comparison of the Stroop effect between the students tested in 2013 and in 2014.

- The **good** paper, <https://github.com/Lakens/stroop_effect_paper>, computes every reported number in its analysis code. The manuscript is a Quarto document, so the text prints these numbers directly from the analysis.
- The **bad** paper, <https://github.com/Lakens/stroop_effect_paper_bad>, has several common mistakes deliberately built in. The results were typed into the text by hand, the shared data contain a value the authors removed before their own analysis without saying so, some reported results are not computed by the code at all, and the code stops with an error before it reaches the last analysis.

## Running the code locally, or using our server on SURF

The reproducibility check runs code that other people wrote. That is not without risk. A script can delete files, read files that have nothing to do with the project, or send information over the internet, by accident or on purpose. By default, `execute = TRUE` runs each script in a separate R process on your own computer. This prevents a script that crashes from taking your own R session down with it, but the script can still reach every file on your computer, and the internet. That is fine for the two repositories in this chapter, which we made ourselves, but not for code from a repository you have not created, as a bad actor might insert problematic code.

For such code, add `sandbox = "docker"`. [Docker](https://www.docker.com/) is a program that runs software in a *container*: a closed environment on your computer, separated from the rest of the system. Metacheck runs every script in its own container, and has set up these containers so that the code can do as little harm as possible:

- The container has no internet connection while the code runs, unless you allow it with `internet = TRUE` (see [Scripts that download their data](#internet)). Only the step before it, which installs the packages the code needs, is connected to the internet, and in that step none of the paper's own code runs.
- The code runs on a copy of the repository's files, in a temporary folder. That folder, and the folder of packages installed for this paper, which is removed after the check, are the only places it can write to, and the files on the rest of your computer are not visible inside the container.
- The code runs as an ordinary user without administrator rights, cannot obtain extra rights, and can start only a limited number of processes.
- Each script is stopped after a time limit, 10 minutes by default.

No sandbox makes running unknown code completely safe: a flaw in Docker itself could in principle still be exploited. But these settings close off the usual ways in which a script can do damage. [Two ways to run the code](#two-ways-to-run-the-code) below lists the exact settings, and compares them with running code without Docker.

Running the check in Docker takes some preparation, and disk space. You need Docker Desktop (on Windows and macOS) or Docker Engine (on Linux), and the space Docker Desktop itself needs. The first time you run the check, Docker downloads Metacheck's image for R code: R, Quarto, and the roughly 750 R packages that occurred in a scan of thousands of R files shared with psychology papers, together about 4.9 GB. Python code runs in a second image of about 2.7 GB. Because most packages a paper needs are already in the image, they do not have to be installed again for every paper, which makes the check much faster (but at the expense of a large docker image that you install once). [The pre-built Docker image](#the-pre-built-docker-image-and-why-it-exists) below explains how it was built.

If you do not use R, the [Docker installation](get-started.qmd#docker-installation) runs Metacheck's website on your own computer, with the same checks. It needs about 1.7 GB of disk space and a computer with 8 GB of memory, plus Docker. There, the code of a repository runs inside Metacheck's own container: it cannot reach the files on your computer, but unlike in the sandbox described above, it can use the internet. The packages the code needs are downloaded while the check runs. Running the check on your own computer also means that an unpublished manuscript never leaves it, which matters for editors and reviewers who may not upload a submission to an external server.

The easiest way to try the check is our server on SURF Research Cloud, which runs on the servers of SURF, the cooperative of the Dutch universities, in the Netherlands. You need nothing but a web browser. On [Metacheck's website](https://metacheckserve.metacheck.src.surf-hosted.nl/), upload a PDF under *Run Metacheck on a Paper* and tick *Also run the code in the paper's repository*, or, under *Run Metacheck on a Repository*, choose a folder or a .zip file, or paste a link to an online repository such as GitHub or OSF; there, running the code is ticked by default. The [ResearchBox Check](https://metacheckserve.metacheck.src.surf-hosted.nl/researchbox/) and the [TU/e Data Manager Check](https://metacheckserve.metacheck.src.surf-hosted.nl/datamanager/) run the check too. The server already has the most common R and Python packages. It first installs any other packages the code needs from CRAN or PyPI, but not packages from GitHub or other links, and then runs each script for at most 5 minutes, in a closed sandbox without internet access. Uploaded files are deleted as soon as they have been read, and the report is kept on the server for one hour, so save it if you want to keep it.

The server's capacity is shared by everyone who uses it, so it is meant for checking a paper or a repository now and then. If you want to check many papers, run Metacheck on your own computer, or [build your own server on SURF Research Cloud](get-started.qmd#your-own-server-on-surf-research-cloud), which researchers at Dutch institutions can do through their institution or with a free NWO grant. The [Setting up Metacheck](get-started.qmd) chapter describes all these options.

## Running the check in R

We illustrate the module in R. Metacheck reads a paper from its PDF. We download both PDFs from GitHub, and `convert()` turns each into a structured file that `read()` loads into R. If you want to follow along in the Metacheck website, download the two papers from [here](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Lakens/stroop_effect_paper/main/output/analysis.pdf) and [here](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Lakens/stroop_effect_paper_bad/main/analysis.pdf). 


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
download.file(
  "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Lakens/stroop_effect_paper/main/output/analysis.pdf",
  destfile = "good_paper.pdf", mode = "wb"
)
download.file(
  "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Lakens/stroop_effect_paper_bad/main/analysis.pdf",
  destfile = "bad_paper.pdf", mode = "wb"
)
paper <- read(convert(file_path = "good_paper.pdf", save_path = "."))
bad_paper <- read(convert(file_path = "bad_paper.pdf", save_path = "."))
```
:::




Both papers link to their repository. The [repo_check](mod-repo-check.qmd) module in Metacheck supports over 270 data repositories, and can automatically download files from these repositories.

Running the module is a single line. By default, `reproducibility_check` only inspects the code without running it. `execute = TRUE` is needed to actually run the full computational reproducibility check:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
mo_good <- module_run(paper, "reproducibility_check", execute = TRUE)
mo_good$traffic_light
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1] "green"
```


:::
:::



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
cat(mo_good$summary_text)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> 
#> -  We assessed AND ran 2 R code files for reproducibility (each in an isolated subprocess).
#> -  2 of 2 scripts ran without error when executed.
#> -  5 installable dependencies detected.
#> - 39 statistics stored from the extracted output; 11 of 11 reported tests matched (100%).
```


:::
:::


The light is green: every script ran without an error, and every result reported in the manuscript was among the results the code produced when it ran. `mo_good$table` lists each script and what happened when it was run:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
mo_good$table[, c("file_name", "outcome")]
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#>                 file_name outcome
#> analysis.qmd analysis.qmd  ran_ok
#> clean_data.R clean_data.R  ran_ok
```


:::
:::


`clean_data.R` turns the raw data file into the processed data file, and `analysis.qmd` is the manuscript, whose code chunks contain the analysis. The repository also contains `renv/activate.R`, a script the `renv` package adds to a project to set up its package library. The module does not check the contents of this folder, because it knows it is not part of the analysis.

`mo_good$match_table` shows, for each result reported in the paper, whether it was found in the output of the code, and in which analysis:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
mo_good$match_table[, c("reported", "found", "confidence", "analysis")] |>
  knitr::kable()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}


|reported                      |found |confidence |analysis                             |
|:-----------------------------|:-----|:----------|:------------------------------------|
|M=15.1                        |TRUE  |full       |mean by group                        |
|M=23                          |TRUE  |full       |mean by group                        |
|SD=4.1                        |TRUE  |full       |sd by group                          |
|SD=4.78                       |TRUE  |full       |sd by group                          |
|r=0.37 t=4.53 df=129 p=<0.001 |TRUE  |full       |Pearson's product-moment correlation |
|t=18.04 df=130 p=<0.001       |TRUE  |full       |Paired t-test                        |
|Cohen's dz=1.58               |TRUE  |full       |d_z                                  |
|M=7.77                        |TRUE  |full       |mean by group                        |
|M=8.13                        |TRUE  |full       |mean by group                        |
|t=-0.42 df=120.37 p=0.673     |TRUE  |full       |Welch Two Sample t-test              |
|Cohen's d=-0.07               |TRUE  |full       |Cohens_d                             |


:::
:::


A result is not compared as single numbers, but as a whole: the *t*-value, the degrees of freedom, and the *p*-value of one test have to appear together in the output of one analysis. Any single number will sooner or later turn up somewhere in a large output by coincidence, but several numbers of one test appearing together in one analysis will not.

::: callout-tip
## Making your own results findable

The module can only find a result if the code produces it while it runs, in a form the module recognises. In the good paper, every reported number is computed in a code chunk, and the text of the manuscript only rounds these values. A number that is computed only inside the text, by an inline R expression in Quarto or R Markdown, is not part of the code that is run, so it cannot be found.

The module recognises the results of test functions such as `t.test()` and `cor.test()`, of summaries such as `sapply(stroop_data[, c("congruent", "incongruent")], mean)`, and of effect sizes from the `effectsize` package, also when they are stored in a variable (`ttest_result <- t.test(...)`). A number computed by hand, such as a Cohen's *d* computed as `mean(diff) / sd(diff)`, is found when the code prints it, but not when it is only stored in a variable.
:::

A green light means that the numbers in the paper follow from the shared code and data. It does not mean that the analysis was the right one to perform.

Now let's see what the module returns if we run it on the bad paper:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
mo_bad <- module_run(bad_paper, "reproducibility_check", execute = TRUE)
mo_bad$traffic_light
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1] "red"
```


:::
:::



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
cat(mo_bad$summary_text)
```

```

#> -  We assessed AND ran 1 R code file for reproducibility (each in an isolated subprocess).
#> -  0 of 1 script ran without error when executed.
#> -  3 installable dependencies detected.
#> - 10 statistics stored from the extracted output; 2 of 6 reported tests matched (33.3%).
```


:::
:::


The light is red, because the analysis code stopped with an error:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
mo_bad$table[, c("file_name", "outcome")]
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
cat(mo_bad$run_results$error)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> ! in callr subprocess.
#> Caused by error in `eval(predvars, data, env)`:
#> ! object 'stroop_effect' not found
```


:::
:::


The code compares the Stroop effect between the two years using a column `stroop_effect`, but no line of the code creates that column. The authors presumably created it in their R console while they worked, so the code ran on their own computer, but it cannot run for anyone else. This is one of the most common reasons shared code fails.

Before the code was run, the module also changed one line of it. `mo_bad$modifications` lists every change:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
mods <- mo_bad$modifications
mods[mods$change_type == "setwd_removed", c("change_type", "detail")]
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#>     change_type                                detail
#> 2 setwd_removed C:/Users/dlakens/Desktop/stroop_study
```


:::
:::


The code starts with `setwd("C:/Users/dlakens/Desktop/stroop_study")`, which sets the folder R works in to a folder that only exists on the author's computer. The module skips this line, and reports that it did, because it would stop the code on any other computer.

Now the comparison between the paper and the output:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
mo_bad$match_table[, c("reported", "found", "confidence", "analysis")] |>
  knitr::kable()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}


|reported                              |found |confidence |analysis      |
|:-------------------------------------|:-----|:----------|:-------------|
|t=18.04 df=130 p=0.25 Cohen's dz=0.25 |FALSE |none       |NA            |
|t=-0.42 df=120.37 p=0.673             |FALSE |none       |NA            |

|SD=4.1                                |TRUE  |full       |sd by group   |
|M=23 SD=4.78                          |FALSE |none       |NA            |
|r=0.37                                |FALSE |none       |NA            |


:::
:::


Only the mean and standard deviation of the congruent condition were found. Each of the other results is missing for a different reason:

- **The incongruent mean and standard deviation** (*M* = 23.0, *SD* = 4.78) are not in the output. The output contains the statistics the code did compute:


  ::: {.cell}
  
  ```{.r .cell-code}
  mo_bad$stat_output[[1]]$long[, c("analysis", "statistic", "value")]
  ```
  
  ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
  
  ```
  #>         analysis       statistic                value
  #> 1  mean by group            mean     15.1102878787879
  #> 2  mean by group            mean      22.080446969697
  #> 3    sd by group              sd     4.08488216267072
  #> 4    sd by group              sd       11.63934788467
  #> 5  Paired t-test               t     6.77356838604279
  #> 6  Paired t-test              df                  131
  #> 7  Paired t-test               p 3.84360296105763e-10
  #> 8  Paired t-test mean difference     6.97015909090909
  #> 9  Paired t-test        conf.low     4.93450571703671
  #> 10 Paired t-test       conf.high     9.00581246478147
  ```
  
  
  :::
  :::


  The incongruent mean is 22.08, with a standard deviation of 11.64. The reason is in the data. One participant has a reaction time of -99 in the incongruent condition:


  ::: {.cell}
  
  ```{.r .cell-code}
  bad_data <- read.csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Lakens/stroop_effect_paper_bad/main/stroop.csv")
  summary(bad_data$Incongruent)
  ```
  
  ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
  
  ```
  #>    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
  #>  -99.00   19.27   22.64   22.08   26.10   35.13
  ```
  
  
  :::
  :::


  -99 is a code for a missing value, not a reaction time. The authors removed this participant before computing the results in their paper, but the code they shared does not, so it analyses -99 as if it were a reaction time.
- **The paired *t*-test**, *t*(130) = 18.04, is not found for the same reason: the shared code analyses all 132 participants, including the -99, and gets *t*(131) = 6.77. The reported *p* = .25 and Cohen's *d~z~* = 0.25 would not have matched in any case, because neither is consistent with a *t*-value of 18.04 (the [StatCheck](mod-stat-check.qmd) and [Effect Sizes](mod-stat-effect-size.qmd) modules flag both from the text alone).
- **The correlation**, *r* = 0.37, is reported, but no line of the code computes it.
- **The comparison between the years**, *t*(120.37) = -0.42, *p* = .673, has exactly the numbers the good paper reports, so it is probably correct. But the code stopped with an error before it reached this test, so it cannot be verified from what the authors shared.

The three *p*-values about accuracy (*p* = .07, *p* = .34, and *p* = .000) are not in the table at all. The module only checks a *p*-value that is reported together with its test statistic. Had they been checked, they would not have been found either: the repository contains no accuracy data.

## What it checks

Where [code_check](mod-code-check.qmd) asks *"is this code written well?"*, `reproducibility_check` asks a harder question: **could this code actually be run on this data — and do the numbers it produces match the ones the paper reports?** It is the module that stands closest to the goal of computational reproducibility.

The module works in two phases, and you choose how far to go:

1. A **static phase** (always run) that works out everything a reproduction attempt *would* involve — the dependencies, the file-path rewrites, the run order, the missing inputs — and reports where that attempt is likely to break, **without running any code**.
2. An **execution phase** (opt-in, `execute = TRUE`) that actually **runs the code**, either in a subprocess on your own machine or inside a locked-down Docker container, against a throwaway copy of the data, captures the statistical output it produces, and — together with any self-contained JASP/jamovi files in the deposit — lets you check whether the reported results are reproduced.

Both phases cover R code and Python code. Most of this chapter describes R; [Python code](#python-code) below describes where Python is handled differently.

::: callout-note
This module builds on `repo_check`, `data_check`, and `code_check`, and inherits their **live network calls** to retrieve the repository files. When you have not run `data_check` and `code_check` on the paper first, the module runs them itself. You need an internet connection to run the code below.
:::

## The static phase, without running code

The default is the static phase — it does not run anything. This example reads every repository `demopaper()` links to, so (like the rest of this chapter) it needs those repositories to be reachable; the output below is shown rather than run live, so the chapter does not depend on every linked repository's uptime at render time:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
paper <- demopaper()
mo <- module_run(paper, "reproducibility_check")
mo$traffic_light
#> [1] "yellow"
cat(mo$summary_text)
#>
#> -  We assessed 6 R code files for reproducibility (static analysis; no code was run).
#> -  3 files appear runnable so far (parses, inputs resolve, placeable in the run order).
#> -  26 files skipped as byte-identical duplicates of another file already in the run (the paper links more than one repository/component).
#> -  2 referenced inputs unavailable (0 withheld due to size).
#> -  6 installable dependencies detected.
```
:::


The `table` has one row per R or Python code file, carrying the static assessments as columns (there is no language column; the file extension shows the language):


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
mo$table[, c("file_name", "parses", "run_order", "order_basis",
             "paths_rewritten", "runnable")] |>
  knitr::kable()
```
:::


|               |file_name      |parses | run_order|order_basis | paths_rewritten|runnable |
|:--------------|:--------------|:------|---------:|:-----------|---------------:|:--------|
|test_script.R  |test_script.R  |TRUE   |         5|none        |               0|FALSE    |
|bad.R          |bad.R          |TRUE   |         2|none        |               0|FALSE    |
|bad.Rmd        |bad.Rmd        |TRUE   |         3|none        |               1|FALSE    |
|01.R           |01.R           |TRUE   |         1|numeric     |               0|TRUE     |
|good-example.R |good-example.R |TRUE   |         4|none        |               0|TRUE     |
|utils.R        |utils.R        |TRUE   |         6|none        |               0|TRUE     |

A file is marked `runnable` only when it parses, all of its referenced inputs resolve (they are present, or produced by an earlier script), and it can be placed in the run order. That is a deliberately strict bar for a *static* check: `runnable = FALSE` does not mean the code is broken, it means the module could not confirm, without running it, that everything the script needs is in place. When it *is* `FALSE`, the column `not_runnable_reason` names exactly why — one of `parse_error`, `unplaceable`, or `missing_input`, checked in that priority order — and `unresolved_inputs` names the specific file(s) that could not be resolved. Two further reasons apply only to an R file that does not parse as R: `not_r_content` when its content is not R at all (for example a JSON or HTML file saved with a `.R` extension), and `jags_model` when it is a JAGS/BUGS model definition. Neither counts as a parse error, because the file is not broken R code, and neither is run. Three more reasons name files that are not run as scripts of their own: `defines_functions` (a file that only defines functions, apart from `library()` calls and constants; `used_by` names the scripts that use it), `not_analysis` (a file of software rather than of the paper's analysis, such as a package's own code or tests, a copy of a tool, a web application, or a script a program wrote; `not_analysis_why` says which), and `needs_a_person` (an R file that starts an app, such as a Shiny application). For Python, `python2` marks code written for Python 2.

Two further list-columns, `reads` and `writes`, carry the basenames each script reads and writes (as `repro_file_io()` extracted them) directly on the table — useful if you want the code↔data provenance for a file without recomputing it yourself:

## Worked example: building a small reproducible fixture

To see every static assessment concretely, it helps to build a tiny, self-contained example rather than rely on whatever a real deposit happens to contain. The example below creates two scripts — one that writes an intermediate file, one that reads it back — and a data file.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
tmp <- withr::local_tempdir()

writeLines(c(
  'dat <- read.csv("data.csv")',
  'summ <- data.frame(mean_x = mean(dat$x))',
  'write.csv(summ, "intermediate.csv", row.names = FALSE)'
), file.path(tmp, "0_prep.R"))

writeLines(c(
  'summ <- read.csv("intermediate.csv")',
  'print(summ$mean_x)'
), file.path(tmp, "1_analysis.R"))

writeLines("x,g\n1,a\n2,a\n3,b\n4,b", file.path(tmp, "data.csv"))
```
:::


The rest of the chapter uses these two files, `0_prep.R` and `1_analysis.R`, to demonstrate each static assessment on its own terms.

## The static assessments, function by function

Each static assessment is an exported helper, so you can run it on your own code independently of the module.

### Dependencies: `repro_dependencies()`

`repro_dependencies()` walks R code and returns the distinct packages it loads, tagged with **where each would be installed from** — a distinction `code_check`'s package list does not make. A `library()` call resolves to CRAN by default; a `remotes::install_github("user/repo")` call sets the install source of the package the code loads under that repository's name (with the pinned `@ref` kept when present); packages that ship with R are tagged `base`, because a run never needs to install them; and a bundled list of common **Bioconductor** package names (`edgeR`, `DESeq2`, and similar) is checked so those are tagged `bioc` instead of `cran` — confirmed as the single largest identifiable cause of install failures in a real corpus run, since a Bioconductor-only package is never on CRAN and `install.packages()` simply fails for it unless this distinction is made upfront.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
code_text <- c(
  "library(dplyr)",
  "library(ggplot2)",
  "remotes::install_github('tidyverse/ggplot2@v3.4.0')",
  "x <- stats::sd(1:10)"
)
repro_dependencies(code_text)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#>   package source                      ref  base
#> 1   dplyr   cran                     <NA> FALSE
#> 2 ggplot2 github tidyverse/ggplot2@v3.4.0 FALSE
#> 3 remotes   cran                     <NA> FALSE
#> 4   stats   base                     <NA>  TRUE
```


:::
:::


Note that a namespace-qualified call — `stats::sd(...)` and `remotes::install_github(...)` above — is picked up as a dependency even without an explicit `library()` call; the last row shows `stats` tagged `base`. `repro_dependencies()` also accepts a **list** of per-file character vectors and pools them into one result: when the same package is named both bare (`library(pkg)`) and via an explicit GitHub source somewhere else in the pooled files, the GitHub row wins, since it carries the real install source.

For R code, the dependency list is deliberately **name-only, not version-pinned**: static analysis cannot recover which version of a package was used. (Python code is the exception: see [Python code](#python-code) for how versions are read from a `requirements.txt` or `pyproject.toml`.) This is not a limitation to apologise for — it is the point. A reproduction runs against the *current* versions of these packages, and if it breaks under current versions, that break is itself a finding: it argues that the authors should have pinned their versions.

That said, `reproducibility_check` does not have to guess blindly at what "current" means. As of the version documented in this chapter, [code_check](mod-code-check.qmd) itself checks whether a deposit **declared** its environment at all — see [Declared R versions](#declared-r-versions-and-why-they-matter-for-docker) below, which explains how this feeds directly into the Docker execution path.

### Paths: `repro_rewrite_paths()` {#paths}

A script reads and writes data by relative path — `read_csv("raw/x.csv")`, `saveRDS(m, "../out/model.rds")`. The module runs the code in a copy of the repository as the authors organised it (see [Where the code runs](#two-layouts)), so most such paths work as written. Some do not: an absolute path on the authors' computer, a path from another folder than the one the script runs in, or the name of a file that is elsewhere in the repository. `repro_rewrite_paths()` maps each referenced path to a file in a *plan*, a table with one row per file and the path it has in the copy. Inside the module, that plan is the repository itself, and only a path that does not work is rewritten. The function also accepts another plan, such as the one `psychds_check` makes for a Psych-DS release, as in the example below.

Matching is by **basename**: a script's `../data/x.csv` and the repository's `raw/x.csv` are the same file seen from different working directories, so the prefix is ignored. A name that has no exact match also matches the one file with the same extension and the same name apart from case, spaces and punctuation, so code that reads `relative cover.csv` reads `relative_cover.csv` (repositories such as Dryad change names in this way on deposit); `table$names_corrected` and `$modifications` (`name_corrected`) record such a change. When several files share a basename — a `demographics.csv` in more than one study — the ambiguity is resolved by **study group**: the candidate whose target path is in the same study as the script wins. Only when that still leaves more than one candidate is the reference left unrewritten and flagged as ambiguous, rather than guessed. A path is only changed where it stands in quotes in the code.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
plan <- data.frame(
  file_name = c("demographics.csv", "scores.csv"),
  target_path = c("study-ex1/data/source-demographics_data.csv",
                  "study-ex1/data/source-scores_data.csv"),
  current_path = c("ex1/demographics.csv", "ex1/scores.csv")
)
repro_rewrite_paths('d <- read.csv("data/demographics.csv")',
                    "ex1/analysis.R", plan)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#>                     ref         basename matched
#> 1 data/demographics.csv demographics.csv    TRUE
#>                                        target ambiguous n_candidates is_call
#> 1 study-ex1/data/source-demographics_data.csv     FALSE            1   FALSE
#>   name_in_code name_in_deposit in_join in_here
#> 1         <NA>            <NA>   FALSE   FALSE
```


:::
:::


Two refinements worth knowing about if you inspect this output closely:

- **Genuinely identical plan rows are not treated as ambiguous.** If the same physical file is listed more than once in the plan (which happens when a paper links several mirrored repositories), and every candidate row resolves to the *same* target path, that is not ambiguity — there was only ever one possible answer, and `repro_rewrite_paths()` recognises this rather than flagging it.
- **Mirror duplicates are collapsed by content, not by name**, when you pass `structure_df` (the `data_check` structure table). A paper linking an OSF component and its own "Archive of OSF Storage" snapshot can have the *same* physical file grouped into two different (and mostly wrong) study labels by upstream heuristics; `repro_rewrite_paths()` hashes each candidate's actual bytes first, so byte-identical mirrors count as one candidate rather than several conflicting ones.

### Run order: `repro_file_io()` and `repro_run_order()`

Scripts in a repository usually depend on each other, and running them in the wrong order fails for reasons that have nothing to do with reproducibility. `repro_file_io()` first extracts, for every file, the data it **reads**, the data it **writes**, and the scripts it **sources**:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
code_text_list <- list(
  "0_prep.R"    = readLines(file.path(tmp, "0_prep.R")),
  "1_analysis.R" = readLines(file.path(tmp, "1_analysis.R"))
)
io <- repro_file_io(code_text_list)
io
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#>      file_name            reads           writes sources source_refs
#> 1     0_prep.R         data.csv intermediate.csv                    
#> 2 1_analysis.R intermediate.csv
```


:::
:::


`repro_run_order()` then derives an order from three signals, in decreasing strength:

1. **read-after-write** — if one script writes `intermediate.csv` and another reads it, the writer must run first (a hard data dependency);
2. **`source()` edges** — if A `source()`s B, B must run first;
3. **numeric filename prefixes** — `0_prep.R` before `1_analysis.R`, and also embedded numbering such as `Exp1_02_...` before `Exp2_1_...` (a weak tie-breaker, not a dependency). The numeric key is the *vector* of every digit run anywhere in the filename, not just a leading prefix, so `Exp1_02_preprocessing.R` correctly sorts before `Exp2_1_import.R`.

Python has no equivalent of `source()` that the module follows, so Python scripts are ordered by the first and third signals only. For R, `repro_run_order()` also returns every `source()` link it found, as a data frame in its `"source_edges"` attribute (`from` is the script that is sourced, `to` the script that sources it); when the code is run, the module uses it to run a sourced script only inside the script that sources it (see the outcome `run_by_source` below).

The scripts are then topologically sorted. A dependency **cycle** (A reads a file B writes, and vice versa) cannot be ordered and is reported; so is an **ambiguous** ordering, where nothing — no dependency and no numbering — distinguishes the order of two or more files.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
repro_run_order(io)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#>      file_name order depends_on order_basis
#> 1     0_prep.R     1                numeric
#> 2 1_analysis.R     2   0_prep.R  dependency
```


:::
:::


`0_prep.R` runs first even though its own name sorts it that way anyway — but critically, the `order_basis` column reads `"dependency"`, not `"numeric"`, because the *real* reason is the data dependency: `1_analysis.R` reads `intermediate.csv`, which `0_prep.R` writes. `order_basis` is recorded on the file that has the **incoming** edge (the dependent file), not the file it depends on — so it is `1_analysis.R`'s row that carries `"dependency"` and names `0_prep.R` in `depends_on`.

### Missing inputs: `repro_missing_inputs()` {#missing-inputs}

When a script reads a file that is not present, the reason matters. `repro_missing_inputs()` cross-references each unresolved read against the file plan and the download records, and classifies it as one of:

- `withheld_size` — the file *is* in the repository, but was not downloaded because it exceeded a size cap. This is a size-cap issue, not a reproducibility failure: raising `max_file_size` / `max_download_size` (in [data_check](mod-data-check.qmd)) would fetch it.
- `in_repo_not_downloaded` — listed in the repository but not present locally for another reason.
- `in_archive` — the file is in the repository only inside a `.zip` or `.tar` (for example `data.zip/data/x.csv`), and the code reads it at the path unpacking would give (`data/x.csv`). The reason reads "only inside data.zip; unpack it so the code finds it".
- `absent` — not in the repository at all. The script reads a file the authors did not share (or that an earlier, un-captured step was meant to produce). For such a file, `similar_to` names a file in the repository with a similar name, if there is one, such as the same name with a piece added at its start or end; the report names it, but the module does not use it.

A file that a script writes itself, and then reads back, is not a missing input. Neither is a name the module cannot check before the code runs: a `paste()` or `sprintf()` call that holds a variable, a name with a placeholder such as `{name}.csv`, or a piece of a name such as `_field.csv`.

These are predictions. With `execute = TRUE`, a script with a predicted missing input is still run, because the prediction is often wrong (the file may be read only inside `if (file.exists(...))`, or its name may be built while the script runs), and the run gives the script's real outcome and error. After a run, a predicted missing input only counts for a script that did not run to the end.

This distinction is the reason the static phase is worth running before a manual reproduction attempt: a run that fails because a 3 GB data file was skipped by the size gate is a completely different situation from a run that fails because the input data were never shared, and only the latter is a genuine openness problem.

### Two more static helpers you may not need directly

Two further exported helpers feed the module internally and are rarely called on their own, but are worth knowing about if you are extending the checks:

- **`repro_defined_vars(code_text_list)`** returns, for each R file, the variable names it assigns at its *top level* (not inside a function). This is what powers the corrective re-run for R described below: when a script fails with `object 'x' not found`, the module looks for exactly one other file whose `repro_defined_vars()` result includes `x`, and — if there is exactly one — infers that it must run first.
- **`repro_materialize_layout()`** and **`repro_write_scripts()`** build the throwaway copy of the repository the execution phase actually runs against, and write the path-rewritten scripts into it. You will see their effects described below (the copied files, and the `output/` and `statistical_output/` folders), but you would only call them directly if you were building your own execution pipeline on top of metacheck's static analysis. `repro_write_scripts()`'s `inject_libs` argument adds one or more `library()` calls to the top of a named R script; the corrective re-run uses it.

## Two ways to run the code {#two-ways-to-run-the-code}

Set `execute = TRUE` to actually run the paper's code. A second argument, `sandbox`, decides **where**:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# on this machine, in an isolated subprocess (the default)
mo <- module_run(paper, "reproducibility_check",
                 execute = TRUE, sandbox = "process",
                 install_missing = TRUE, timeout = 600)

# inside a locked-down Docker container
mo <- module_run(paper, "reproducibility_check",
                 execute = TRUE, sandbox = "docker",
                 install_missing = TRUE, timeout = 600)
```
:::


The two options carry genuinely different risk, and the difference is worth understanding precisely rather than taking on faith:

| | `sandbox = "process"` (default) | `sandbox = "docker"` |
|---|---|---|
| Mechanism | a subprocess on your machine: a `callr` R process for an R script, a `python` process for a Python script | a `docker run` container |
| Isolates a crash? | Yes | Yes |
| Isolates the filesystem? | **No** — the code can read, write, or delete anywhere your R session can | **Yes** — `--read-only`, with only the throwaway sandbox directory, the paper's own package library and `/tmp` writable |
| Isolates the network? | **No** — the code can reach the internet freely | **Yes** — `--network none` during the run phase, unless you set `internet = TRUE` |
| Runs as | your own user account | a non-root user inside the container: on Windows and macOS user 1000; on Linux the user running R (user 1000 when R runs as root) |
| Requires | the `callr` package (only when the paper has R code); for Python code, the `processx` package and a Python interpreter (`python`, or else `python3`) | Docker installed and running, plus the `processx` package |
| Speed | fast — no container overhead | pre-built image (see below) makes this close to the process backend for most papers |

`sandbox = "docker"` achieves real containment with these `docker run` flags, applied to every script individually during the run phase:

```
--network none --read-only --tmpfs /tmp:exec
--user <uid:gid> --cap-drop ALL
--security-opt no-new-privileges --pids-limit 512 --ulimit core=1
-v <sandbox>:/sandbox -v <library>:/rlib                       (R)
-v <sandbox>:/sandbox -v <library>:/pylib
   -e PYTHONPATH=<the repository's own module folders>:/pylib     (Python)
```

Network is fully disabled (`--network none` is left out only when you set `internet = TRUE`), the filesystem is read-only outside the mounted sandbox (with only `/tmp`, the sandbox itself, and the library of packages installed for this paper writable), the container runs as a non-root user, all Linux capabilities are dropped, privilege escalation is blocked, the number of processes the container can start is limited, and R cannot write a crash file (on Windows, each R crash in a container wrote a file of about 2.5 GB). Programs in `/tmp` may run, because code that is compiled while a script runs, such as an `rstan` model or `Rcpp::sourceCpp()`, is loaded from there. The library is writable because some packages keep data in their own folder; it belongs to this paper only and is removed after the check. It is kept in a Docker volume rather than in a folder of your computer, because a Windows drive does not tell file names apart by case, and an exFAT drive refuses Linux file permissions; the volume is named after the sandbox and removed with it. The option `options(metacheck.docker_lib_volume = FALSE)` keeps the library in a folder of your computer instead.

The user the containers run as (`<uid:gid>` above) depends on the computer. Docker Desktop on Windows and macOS shares folders with a container without asking who owns them, so there the containers run as user 1000. On Linux only a folder's owner may write in it, so the containers run as the user running R; otherwise, on a computer where R runs as another user (such as a server, or GitHub's Linux machine), installing packages stopped with "Permission denied". When R runs as root, the containers still run as user 1000, not as root, and the folders they write in are opened to that user; symbolic links are left alone, so a link in a deposit cannot open a folder outside it. `options(metacheck.docker_user = "uid:gid")` chooses the user. Before checking any of this, call `repro_docker_available()` to confirm Docker is installed and its daemon is actually running — `reproducibility_check()` calls this for you and stops with a clear message if it is not, rather than failing partway through a batch of papers with a cryptic error. When Docker is slow to answer, because other containers are busy, it asks again, waiting up to 30 and then 60 seconds, and when Docker still does not answer, the message says so instead of saying that Docker is not running. A script whose container never started, or that Docker lost while it ran, gets the outcome `docker_failed`, which says nothing about the script.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
repro_docker_available()
#> $ok
#> [1] TRUE
#> $msg
#> [1] ""
```
:::


::: callout-note
The dependency-install phase under `sandbox = "docker"` runs with the network **on** (it has to, to reach CRAN or GitHub, or for Python code the package index that `pip` installs from) but is otherwise hardened the same way — non-root, capabilities dropped, no new privileges. Only the per-script *run* phase disables the network entirely, since that is the phase running the paper's own, potentially untrusted, analysis code.
:::

::: callout-tip
Working through a whole corpus rather than one paper? [Batch mode](#batch-mode), described later in this chapter, runs several papers' `sandbox = "docker"` checks concurrently instead of one at a time.
:::

## The pre-built Docker image, and why it exists

The first time you think through what `sandbox = "docker"` needs to do to run a real paper's code, an obvious problem appears: most papers' scripts `library()` several packages that are not part of base R, and a container starts with nothing installed. Naively, every single `reproducibility_check()` call would need to install a paper's entire dependency list from scratch, inside a freshly-started container, before it could run a single script — for R packages with compiled C++ code (`rstan`, `lme4`, and dozens of others), that can mean minutes of compilation *per paper*.

To avoid that, Docker containers under `sandbox = "docker"` default to a **pre-built image**, `ghcr.io/scienceverse/metacheck_r_large:latest`, rather than a bare R installation. That image already has R, Quarto, JAGS, Java, the GDAL/GEOS/PROJ libraries for geographic data, and the roughly 750 most common packages a real corpus of psychology-science papers' code actually uses — found by scanning thousands of real `.R`/`.Rmd`/`.qmd` files for their `library()`/`require()` calls and pre-installing everything that showed up often enough to be worth the build cost. When a paper's dependencies are already in that list — which, for an ordinary `tidyverse`-and-`lme4`-shaped analysis, they usually are — the install phase does almost nothing, because `requireNamespace()` already finds the package. Only genuinely uncommon or paper-specific dependencies still need a real, from-source install. A smaller variant, `metacheck_r_small` (about 390 packages, each seen in at least three files of that scan, without the geographic libraries), is also published, but `reproducibility_check()` has no argument to choose it. Python code runs in a separate image, `ghcr.io/scienceverse/metacheck_py_small:latest` by default — see [Python code](#python-code).

When a package is not in the image, the install looks for it in this order: CRAN, Bioconductor, the latest version in the CRAN Archive (for a package CRAN has removed, such as `rgdal`, `rgeos` and `maptools`, which compile when the image has the GDAL and GEOS header files), and then, in Docker only, a table of known places (such as `rethinking` on GitHub or `INLA`'s own repository) and R-universe's search for that exact name. A package that could not be installed is reported with the reason from the install's own output. When the code loads a package that is on neither CRAN nor Bioconductor and does not say where it comes from, the report says so. Only the packages of the files that are run are installed, not those of a package's own code or tests, or of a tool the authors copied into the repository. While it installs, the module shows the package, the count, the time so far and an estimate of the time left.

The container's home folder cannot be written to, so R's cache, configuration and data folders are placed in `/tmp`. This lets a script run `renv::restore()`, which needs to write its cache. `rmarkdown::render()` finds the Pandoc program that Quarto bundles in the image, through the `RSTUDIO_PANDOC` environment variable.

The image, its Dockerfile, the full package list, and detailed notes on how it was built (including some genuinely non-obvious bugs found along the way — a package can report a successful install and still fail to *load*, because a runtime shared library it needs is missing from a minimal image) are all in a dedicated repository: [scienceverse/metacheck_docker_reproducibility](https://github.com/scienceverse/metacheck_docker_reproducibility). If you want to build your own variant — a smaller image with only the most common packages, or one that adds LaTeX for PDF rendering, or CmdStan for `cmdstanr`-based Bayesian models — that repository is the starting point, and its README documents exactly which levers actually reduce image size and which ones (surprisingly) do not.

## Declared R versions, and why they matter for Docker {#declared-r-versions-and-why-they-matter-for-docker}

This section applies to R code only; metacheck does not read a declared Python version, and Python code always runs in the pre-built Python image.

The pre-built image is fast, but it was built against one specific R version. A paper that deposited an `renv.lock` file, or a `sessionInfo()` text dump, or that pins its environment with `groundhog`/`checkpoint`, has told you *exactly* which R version its authors actually used — and that might not be the version the pre-built image happens to run.

[code_check](mod-code-check.qmd) is where this gets detected, as part of its own "Reproducible Environment" check: it looks for an `renv.lock` file anywhere in the repository (parsing its declared R version and every locked package + version), a `sessionInfo()`/`session_info()` dump (matched by filename — `sessionInfo.txt`, `session_info.txt`, and similar — or embedded in a README, or pasted into an R script, usually as comments, when it lists packages; the package versions it lists are kept as well as the R version), or an actual `groundhog::groundhog.library()`/`checkpoint::checkpoint()` date-pin call in the code, also when the date is held in a variable or given as `snapshot_date` — a bare `library(groundhog)` with no pinning call does not count, since loading the package is not evidence anything was actually pinned, and neither does a call in a comment.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
cc <- module_run(paper, "code_check")
cc$traffic_light
#> [1] "yellow"
```
:::


When nothing was declared, `code_check`'s own report explicitly says so and recommends depositing one — this is itself a piece of reproducibility hygiene worth checking regardless of whether you ever run the code.

`reproducibility_check()` has a parameter, `docker_use_declared_version`, that decides what to do with this information:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# default: always use the fast pre-built image, regardless of what the
# paper declared
mo <- module_run(paper, "reproducibility_check",
                 execute = TRUE, sandbox = "docker")

# opt in to matching the paper's own declared R version exactly
mo <- module_run(paper, "reproducibility_check",
                 execute = TRUE, sandbox = "docker",
                 docker_use_declared_version = TRUE)
```
:::


By default (`docker_use_declared_version = FALSE`), the module always uses the pre-built `metacheck_r_large` image, prioritising speed. If the paper *did* declare a version, you get a warning naming the mismatch and explaining how to opt out of it — this is a deliberate design choice: silently running a paper's code against a different R version than the one its authors used could, in principle, change results, and that substitution should never happen invisibly.

```
Warning message:
reproducibility_check(sandbox = "docker"): this paper declared R version
4.3.1, but docker_use_declared_version = FALSE (the default), so the run
uses the pre-built metacheck_r_large image's own R version instead, for speed.
Set docker_use_declared_version = TRUE to match the paper's declared
version exactly -- slower, since every dependency then installs from
scratch rather than using the pre-built image.
```

Setting `docker_use_declared_version = TRUE` switches to a bare `rocker/r-ver:<declared version>` image with nothing pre-installed — genuinely slower, since every dependency now installs from source, but it matches the R version the paper's authors used. When a paper declared *no* version at all, this option falls back to bare `rocker/r-ver:latest` rather than silently reusing the pre-built image either — if you explicitly asked for version-matching, getting the fast pre-built image back through the back door when there was nothing to match against would defeat the point of asking. For an R version before 4.0, whose images name MRAN, a copy of CRAN that closed in 2023, the packages come from the same dated copy of CRAN at Posit.

### Recorded package versions {#recorded-versions}

The R version is one thing; the versions of the packages are another. With `recorded_versions = TRUE` (and `execute = TRUE`), when the repository records package versions — in an `renv.lock` file, in a `sessionInfo()` or `session_info()` record, or as a date in a `groundhog.library()` or `checkpoint()` call — the R packages the scripts load are installed at those versions:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
mo <- module_run(paper, "reproducibility_check",
                 execute = TRUE, sandbox = "docker",
                 recorded_versions = TRUE)
```
:::


This works under both `sandbox` settings, and also when you did not set `install_missing` (see [Options](#options)). Only the packages the scripts load are installed at their recorded version; a loaded package the record does not list gets its current version, and the packages these depend on, and those that come with R, are not at their recorded versions. The R version is not changed, so an old package may not install, or may behave differently; a warning and the report say so. After installing, the module checks in a new R process that each package loads: an old version next to current packages can keep one from loading, as a current `ggplot2` next to a recorded `scales` did. A recorded version that cannot be installed, or that keeps a package from loading, is replaced by the current one, and the report names it. `$recorded_versions` holds which recorded versions the run used.

`recorded_versions = FALSE` is the default, because on 16 repositories this took about 2.7 times as long, and no failing script started working. When scripts fail and the repository records versions, the report, the summary and the checklist recommend a new run with `recorded_versions = TRUE`. Recorded versions are not used when several papers run as one; run the papers one at a time, or in [batch mode](#batch-mode).

When packages are installed before the run, or the run is in Docker, where the network is off, a script's calls to `groundhog`, `checkpoint` and `renv` would fail, so they are replaced: `groundhog.library()` becomes `library()`, and `renv::restore()` and the like become a statement that does nothing. `$modifications` records this as `env_call_replaced`, and the report says so.

## Checking many papers at once: batch mode {#batch-mode}

Everything so far runs one paper through `reproducibility_check()` at a time. If you are working through a whole corpus — a `paperlist` of dozens or hundreds of papers — calling it once per paper in a loop means only one Docker container is ever running: paper 2 does not start until paper 1's containers (install, then run) have both finished. For `sandbox = "docker"`, where each paper's own work is a slow, external `docker run` rather than in-memory R computation, that is time left on the table on any machine with more than one CPU core to spare.

Passing a `paperlist` together with `workers > 1` (and `execute = TRUE, sandbox = "docker"`) switches to **batch mode**: up to `workers` papers run their Docker checks at the same time, and the moment one paper finishes, the next paper in the list starts — never fewer than `workers` running while papers remain queued, never more.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
papers <- papers_load("psychsci", cache = TRUE)[1:20]

mo <- module_run(papers, "reproducibility_check",
                 execute = TRUE, sandbox = "docker",
                 workers = 4, timeout = 600,
                 results_dir = "repro_results")
```
:::


A few things are worth understanding about how this actually runs, rather than treating it as a black box:

- **Each paper runs in its own background R process** (via the `callr` package — install it if it is not already present), not in your current R session. This is deliberate, not an implementation detail you can ignore: `reproducibility_check()` reads and restores a few process-wide settings during a single-paper call (`llm_use()`, an internal option `data_check`/`code_check` share for API-limit handling), and those are not safe for several papers to set and restore *concurrently* in one shared session. A separate OS process per paper sidesteps the problem entirely — one paper's settings can never be observed by another's. Every `metacheck.*` option you have set in your own session (for example the cache directory) is copied into each background process, so each paper's run uses the same settings yours would.
- **Every other argument still means exactly what it means for one paper.** `timeout`, `install_missing`, `docker_use_declared_version`, `cache`, and everything else in [Options](#options) apply individually to each paper's own run; `workers` only controls how many of those individual runs are in flight together.
- **Container resource limits scale with `workers` automatically.** Each container is capped at `1/workers` of the host's CPU and memory (`--cpus`, `--memory`, in addition to the `--pids-limit 512` every container already had) — so four concurrent papers cannot collectively claim more than the whole machine, and one runaway script cannot starve the other three. You do not set this yourself; it is computed from `workers` and the host's own detected CPU count and RAM.
- **`results_dir` writes each paper's full result to disk as soon as that paper finishes** — one `<paper_id>.rds` file per paper, in the same format `capture_module_tables()` uses elsewhere in Metacheck for a corpus build. This matters for a batch that might take hours: if it is interrupted partway through (a crash, a machine restart, you stopping it deliberately), every paper that had already finished is safely on disk, not lost along with the ones still running. Read them back with `metacheck:::collect_module_tables("repro_results", "reproducibility_check")` — both `capture_module_tables()` and `collect_module_tables()` are internal helpers, not exported, so they need the `metacheck:::` prefix rather than a plain call.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
mo$summary_table[, c("paper_id", "repro_ran_ok", "repro_deps")] |> head()
mo$summary_text
#> Ran the reproducibility check on 20 papers (up to 4 at a time): 17 ok, 2 red, 1 error.
```
:::


The returned object has the same shape as a single-paper call, just with one row per paper in `$table` and `$summary_table` (tagged by `paper_id`, exactly like every other module that accepts a `paperlist`), plus one extra element: `$per_paper`, a named list holding each paper's own complete, untruncated module result — the full `$run_results`, `$install_results`, `$stat_output`, and `$report` you would get from calling `reproducibility_check()` on that paper alone.

::: callout-note
Batch mode is specific to `sandbox = "docker"`. Passing `workers > 1` with `sandbox = "process"`, with `execute = FALSE`, or with a single paper does nothing different — those paths are already fast enough, or already isolate only at the crash level rather than the process level, that running several at once is not worth the added complexity of a background-process pool. `workers` is simply ignored in those cases rather than raising an error, so a script that loops over papers with mixed settings does not need to branch on it itself.
:::

## Running the code: what happens during execution

Whichever `sandbox` you choose, the mechanics are the same:

1. **copies the repository's files** into a throwaway temporary directory (see [Where the code runs](#two-layouts) below), so the run never touches your real archive or the download cache. The files the code names are downloaded with the others, also when `download` would leave them out;
2. **writes the path-rewritten scripts** into that copy, so their reads and writes resolve;
3. optionally **installs the declared dependencies** into a throwaway library (`install_missing = TRUE`, or recorded versions, see [Recorded package versions](#recorded-versions)), never your main R library — under `sandbox = "docker"` this is *always* into a throwaway library for the container, since a container has no access to your host library at all. Python packages are installed with `pip` into a throwaway folder in the same way (with `pip install --target` under `sandbox = "process"`, and with `pip install --prefix` inside the container under `sandbox = "docker"`, so that `pip` uses the packages the image already has). `install_timeout` limits the time for installing, R and Python together;
4. **runs each script in run order**, each in its own subprocess or container with a per-script `timeout`, capturing the outcome and the console output. An R script that another script runs with `source()` is not run on its own, but only as part of the script that sources it, and the same holds for a Python file that other files import. Every script that parses is run, also when an input it seems to need was predicted to be missing (see [Missing inputs](#missing-inputs)).


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
mo <- module_run(paper, "reproducibility_check",
                 execute = TRUE, install_missing = TRUE,
                 timeout = 600, keep_sandbox = TRUE)
```
:::


### Where the code runs {#two-layouts}

The module always runs the code in a copy of the repository as the authors organised it. Earlier versions could also run it in a reorganised Psych-DS copy, chosen with a `layout` argument; that argument is gone, because a run in a reorganised copy says little about whether the authors' own deposit works.

Every file the run has (every file of a local folder; for a repository, every file that was downloaded, see `download`) is copied to its own path, so a path that works in the repository works in the copy. Each script runs from the folder where its paths work, which is not always the top of the repository, since the folder the authors ran it from is not recorded. Only a path that cannot work as written is rewritten: an absolute path on the author's computer or a path out of the repository, to the file with that name; a path that counts from the script's own folder (`source("helpers.R")`, `"../data/x.csv"`) or from its RStudio project's (`.Rproj`) folder, to the file's path from the top of the repository; a path to a file at the top of the repository, from a script that runs in a folder below; and a bare file name read directly, as in `read.csv("x.csv")`, to the one file of that name in a folder below. A path that is the one argument of `here()` counts from the folder `here()` starts in. A Windows path (`"Data\\x.txt"`) gets `/` between its folders, since on Linux a backslash is part of a file name. This also applies to files the code makes: a script in `Study 2/` writing `"Data/processed.csv"` writes into `Study 2/Data/`. Any other relative path is left as written, also when other files share its name, since code commonly joins it with a folder of its own. A script's writes stay where the code puts them, so a later script reads the file where it expects it (only a write to an absolute path or out of the repository goes to `output/`), and the copied files are writable, so a script can save over a file the repository holds. The folder of a write is made when it does not exist, also when the folder is held in a variable (`dirF <- "../Figures/"` with `ggsave(paste0(dirF, "plot.png"))`).


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
module_run(NULL, "reproducibility_check", local_path = "path/to/folder",
           execute = TRUE)
```
:::


### Time limits

`timeout` limits each script (600 seconds by default). `total_timeout` limits all scripts together, R and Python: by default one hour (3600 seconds), counted from when the first script starts. Use `NULL` or `Inf` for no limit, or give a clock time (`POSIXct`) by which all scripts must be done, such as a server's job limit minus the time its report needs. Once the time has run out, a running script is stopped and no further script is started, so a package with many slow scripts still gets a report. A script that was not started gets the outcome `skipped_time_limit`, which the report names, and the light is then at least yellow. A script that a later run (see [Running scripts again](#running-again) below) was to run with a change, but which had no time left, is also `skipped_time_limit`, not the first run's failure that the change was meant to fix. In the first run, a script stopped by `total_timeout` is `timed_out`.

To find the statistical results in what a script printed, the module searches only the first 20,000 lines of each script's printed output, and the report says when it stopped there. The search reads about 700 lines a second, so a script that prints a growing table in a loop could otherwise take longer to search than to run. Set another number with `options(metacheck.repro_output_max_lines = ...)`.

### Scripts that download their data {#internet}

Some scripts download their data while they run. In Docker the network is off while the code runs, so such a script stops, with the outcome `needs_internet`. `internet = TRUE` (or `options(metacheck.repro_internet = TRUE)`) lets the scripts use the internet, under `sandbox = "docker"` only. What they download follows the limits for the repository's own files: a script is stopped, with the outcome `download_too_large`, when the paper's scripts together have downloaded more than `max_download_size`, or when a file larger than `max_file_size` appears. The report then says that the scripts could use the internet, so what they downloaded may differ from what the authors had. `internet = FALSE` is the default, because nobody has checked the code before it runs. With `sandbox = "process"` scripts always have the internet, without these limits.

### Outcomes

Each script gets one outcome, in the `outcome` column of `$table` and `$run_results`:

| Outcome | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `ran_ok` | the script ran to completion without error |
| `errored` | the script raised an error (captured, with the message and output) |
| `timed_out` | still running at the `timeout` cutoff — **not** a failure, just slow; raise `timeout` for legitimately long analyses (e.g. Bayesian sampling) |
| `not_parsed` | not run, because the script does not parse (for Python, checked with Python's own parser) |
| `python2` | Python code written for Python 2 (a `print` or `exec` statement, `except E, e`, or tabs mixed with spaces). Under `sandbox = "docker"` it runs with Python 2.7, in the official image `python:2.7-slim` (option `metacheck.docker_image_py2`; `FALSE` turns this off), with, when packages are installed, the last versions of its packages that support Python 2, and then gets the outcome of that run. The code is never converted, since that can change results |
| `dependency_unavailable` | not run (or failed immediately), because a package the script needs is missing: when packages are installed, it could not be installed from any source the install tries (see [The pre-built Docker image](#the-pre-built-docker-image-and-why-it-exists)); when they are not, it is simply not installed on the computer or in the container that ran the script. Either way this is a limitation of where the code ran, not a defect in the paper's code. For Python: the script stopped with `No module named ...` for a package `pip` could not install, or that was not installed |
| `not_downloaded` | the script stopped on a file the repository lists but that was not downloaded, such as one over `max_file_size`. It could not be tried, so it is not counted as a script that did not reproduce |
| `needs_a_person` | the script stopped because it asks a person to choose a file or answer a question, or because it is a program that needs arguments from the person who runs it (R's `commandArgs()`, Python's `sys.argv` or `argparse`), or it starts an app, a window or a server, which would wait for a person until the time limit; such an app is not run |
| `needs_internet` | the script stopped because the network is off in a Docker run, or, with `internet = TRUE`, could not reach what it asked for |
| `download_too_large` | the script was stopped for downloading more than the limits allow (see [Scripts that download their data](#internet)) |
| `out_of_memory` | the script, or a program it started (such as a compiler), ran out of the memory each script may use |
| `docker_failed` | the script's container never started, or Docker lost it while it ran; this says nothing about the script |
| `skipped_time_limit` | not started, or, in a later run, stopped early, because `total_timeout` had run out (see [Time limits](#time-limits)) |
| `run_by_source` | an R script that another script runs with `source()`. It is run only inside that script, because on its own it lacks the packages and objects the sourcing script sets up first; its result is part of that script's result. A sourced script that does not parse keeps its own outcome instead |
| `run_by_import` | a Python file that other files import, such as `utils/data_handling.py`: a module that defines functions for the scripts that import it, which fails or does nothing on its own. It is not run, and not counted among the scripts that ran. A file with an `if __name__ == "__main__":` block still runs. Only `.py` files count as imported |
| `defines_functions` | a file that only defines functions (apart from `library()` calls and constants); it is used by the scripts that load it (`used_by` names them), not run on its own |
| `not_analysis` | a file of software rather than of the paper's analysis: a package's own code, tests or documentation, a copy of a tool, a web application, a script a program wrote (`not_analysis_why` says which). It is not run and not counted as a script |
| `jags_model`, `not_r_content` | a JAGS or BUGS model saved with an R extension, which another script reads, or a file with an R extension that is not R at all; not run, and not failures |

`dependency_unavailable` is deliberately **excluded** from forcing the traffic light red, unlike `errored`/`timed_out` — a package that has genuinely vanished from every source metacheck tries is not evidence the paper's own analysis is broken. `not_downloaded`, `needs_a_person`, `needs_internet`, `download_too_large`, `out_of_memory`, `docker_failed` and `skipped_time_limit` do not make the light red either, but keep it from being green.

For each script that did not run to the end, the `reason` column of `$table` and `$run_results` says why, in one word, taken from the error that stopped the script (not from a warning before it): `file` (a file it could not open), `package` (a missing package), `undefined` (an object or function that was never defined), `syntax`, `environment` (something the computer that ran it lacks, such as a program the code starts, a screen, or memory; the report names a missing program), `internet`, `download`, `interactive`, `time`, `no_message` (the script stopped without a message), or `other`. `$summary_table` counts the scripts per reason. The `error_message` column of `$table` gives the error itself, in at most 300 characters, for R and Python scripts: the error line of the script's output, as the report shows it (which names a package that is not there), with the address the script asked for when it needed the internet and the error line names none, or the time limit it reached; when there is no error line, the last line of the output. For example: `Error in .Primitive(":")() : 0 arguments passed to ':' which requires 2`.

### Running scripts again {#running-again}

Two R errors lead to one corrective re-run. An error whose message is `object '...' not found` usually means the script expects a variable another script defines. When exactly one other script in the repository defines that variable — checked via `repro_defined_vars()` — the module places that script first (adding a "definer runs first" edge and re-sorting), and, because each script has an R session of its own, runs the defining script at the start of the failing script's session (recorded in `$modifications` as `loaded_first`). Authors often run scripts one after another in one session, so that one script's objects are there for the next. An error whose message is `could not find function "..."`, for a function no script of the paper defines, usually means a package was never loaded. The module then adds `library()` calls to the top of the failing script: all the packages the project's other scripts load, when one of them provides the function (such a script was usually written to run after those scripts, in the same R session); otherwise the one package, among the paper's own dependencies and a short list of very common packages, that exports the function; otherwise, for `%>%`, magrittr. Each added call is recorded in `$modifications`, and a script that then runs is reported as reproducible only after adding `library()` calls it should make itself. This second run runs only what it changes: the scripts that got `library()` lines or another script to load first, the scripts the new order moves, and the scripts that read what those write. An unchanged script keeps its first result, so a script that ran out of time does not use the paper's time a second time. These two repairs are decided only once, from the errors of the first run: a second such error after that is accepted as the final result rather than chased indefinitely.

Some scripts then run once more, each for a reason of its own:

- A script that stopped on a default of R that has changed since the code was written — before R 4.0, `read.csv()`, `read.table()` and `data.frame()` read text as factors — runs once more with the old default set at its top (`old_default`), and so do the scripts that stopped on a file it writes.
- A file a script could not open, which the repository lists but which was not downloaded, is downloaded then, and the scripts that stopped on it run once more.
- A script that stopped on a file another script wrote later in the run runs once more (`run_again`): a name built while a script runs, such as `paste0("input", i, ".txt")`, cannot be seen before the run, so the order missed it. A file written in another folder is copied to where the script looked (`output_copied`).
- A script that stopped on a file the repository holds in another folder gets a copy of that file where it looked, and runs once more (`file_placed`). This covers a path built while the script runs, with `file.path()`, `paste0()` or a variable, which cannot be rewritten beforehand.

A script runs once more each time it stops on a file it did not stop on before, up to five times: a figure script that loads the files of four analysis scripts stops on each of them in turn. These later runs apply to R and Python scripts alike, except the one with R's old defaults. A Python script that fails with a `NameError` is not run again; see [Python code](#python-code).

::: callout-note
Two habits in shared code are handled automatically. A `setwd()` call in R, or an `os.chdir()` call in Python — which hardcodes where the code must run and would override the sandbox — is replaced before the script runs by a statement that does nothing (`invisible(NULL)` in R, `pass` in Python), with the original call kept in a comment beside it, so a block that held only that call still has a statement. This also applies to `base::setwd()` and to `chdir()` under any module name (`from os import chdir`, or `o.chdir()` after `import os as o`). Each change is recorded in `$modifications`, and the report notes that the script is "reproducible after ignoring a `setwd()` that should not have been in the code" (or an `os.chdir()`). An SPSS data file (`.sav`/`.zsav`/`.por`) with **no** accompanying syntax (`.sps`) turns the light red, because that analysis cannot be reproduced from the deposit; the same is true for a Stata `.dta` file with no `.do`. This holds whatever language the paper's code is in, also when the paper has only Python code. The report recommends depositing analyses as jamovi or JASP files instead, since those bundle data and analyses together and need no code to be re-run at all.
:::

::: callout-note
Byte-identical duplicate files are only run once. A paper that links several repository components mirroring the same materials — a "live" OSF component, an "Archive of OSF Storage" snapshot, a view-only anonymised link — would otherwise have `code_check` list the *same* script once per mirror, and the module would run it two, four, or more times for no reason. `reproducibility_check` hashes each resolved script's actual content and drops exact duplicates before running, naming which kept file each dropped one mirrors in the report.
:::

## Python code {#python-code}

Python code goes through the same two phases as R code, and the report describes it in its own section, headed "Python code", after the R sections. A `.py` file is Python code, and so is a Jupyter notebook (`.ipynb`) or Quarto document (`.qmd`) whose code is Python (`code_check` reads a notebook's declared kernel, and a Quarto document's declared engine or else its first code chunk). The code in a notebook or Quarto document is taken out of it first, so that `python` runs the code and not the notebook's JSON text or the document's Markdown.

The static phase differs from R in three ways:

- **Syntax check.** Each file is read by Python's own parser, which checks the syntax without running the code. This needs a Python interpreter (`python`, or else `python3`) on your computer; without one, every file is counted as parsing and the report says that the check could not be done. Code written for Python 2 (for example `print "x"`) gets the outcome `python2` instead of counting as a parse error, and is run with Python 2.7 under `sandbox = "docker"` (see [Outcomes](#outcomes)).
- **Dependencies.** `repro_dependencies_py()` reads the packages from the `import` lines. Modules of Python's standard library are tagged `base`, the rest `pypi`. When the name a package is imported under differs from the name `pip` installs, the `pip` name is reported: `sklearn` becomes `scikit-learn`, `cv2` becomes `opencv-python`, `PIL` becomes `Pillow`, `yaml` becomes `PyYAML`, `bs4` becomes `beautifulsoup4`, and so on for about twenty such names. Unlike for R, versions can be known: when the repository has a `requirements.txt` (or, if not, a `pyproject.toml`), the requirement it states for a package is kept in `ref` and used when installing it.
- **Run order.** Python scripts are ordered by read-after-write and by the numbers in their filenames only.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
code_text <- c(
  "import numpy as np",
  "from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression",
```
